items.new: Walk around the city on a dreamy Sunday afternoon. Go from Corlears Hook to Coenties Slip and then north by way of Whitehall. What do you see? Standing like silent sentinels all around the town are thousands upon thousands of mortal men fixed in ocean reveries. Some lean against the pilings; some sit on the pier heads; some gaze over the sides of ships from China; some perch high in the rigging, trying to get an even better view of the sea. But these are all landlocked people — weekdays they're penned up in plaster and wood, chained to counters, nailed to benches, clamped to desks. What's going on? Have all the green fields vanished? What are they doing here?

items.new: Now, when I say I go to sea whenever my eyes grow hazy and I become too aware of my own breathing, don't imagine I ever go as a passenger. To go as a passenger you need a purse, and a purse is just a rag unless there's something in it. Besides, passengers get seasick, grow quarrelsome, don't sleep at night, and generally don't enjoy themselves much. No, I never go as a passenger; nor, though I know my way around a ship, do I ever go as a Commodore, Captain, or Cook. I leave the glory of such positions to those who want them. I personally despise all honorable, respectable labor, trials, and tribulations. I have quite enough to do just looking after myself without looking after ships, barques, brigs, and schooners. And as for going as cook — though I confess there's considerable glory in that, a cook being a sort of officer on board — I never much liked the idea of broiling chickens. Though once broiled, properly buttered, judiciously salted and peppered, there's no one who speaks of a broiled chicken with more respect — even reverence — than I do. It's because of the ancient Egyptians' idolatrous doting on broiled ibis and roasted hippopotamus that you find mummies of those creatures in their enormous bake-houses, the pyramids.

items.new: I sat down on an old wooden bench carved all over like a seat on the Battery. At one end, a ruminative sailor was further decorating it with his jackknife, stooping over and working diligently at the space between his knees. He was attempting a ship under full sail, but he wasn't making much headway, I thought.

items.new: But Queequeg sat among them — at the head of the table, as it happened — cool as an icicle. To be sure, I can't say much for his breeding. His greatest admirer couldn't have heartily justified his bringing the harpoon to breakfast and using it without ceremony — reaching across the table with it, endangering many heads, and hooking the beefsteaks toward himself. But that he certainly did very coolly, and everyone knows that in most people's estimation, to do anything coolly is to do it genteelly.
